rows.label: physical measurement
rows.correct: A measurement is a numerical value accompanied by a unit and compares a quantity with an accepted standard.
wrong: A numerical value without a unit is a complete measurement of every physical quantity.
rows.explanation: A measurement is a numerical value accompanied by a unit and compares a quantity with an accepted standard.

rows.label: SI base quantities
rows.correct: The SI has seven base quantities; other mechanical and electromagnetic units can be derived from them.
wrong: Force and energy are SI base quantities.
rows.explanation: The SI has seven base quantities; other mechanical and electromagnetic units can be derived from them.

rows.label: coherent derived units
rows.correct: A coherent derived SI unit follows from base units without an additional numerical factor.
wrong: Every unit conversion changes the physical quantity being measured.
rows.explanation: A coherent derived SI unit follows from base units without an additional numerical factor.

rows.label: unit conversion by dimensions
rows.correct: A physical quantity is unchanged when its unit is changed, so its numerical value changes inversely with unit size.
wrong: The numerical value and unit size change in the same direction.
rows.explanation: A physical quantity is unchanged when its unit is changed, so its numerical value changes inversely with unit size.

rows.label: order-of-magnitude conversion
rows.correct: Prefixes represent powers of ten and must be applied to the whole measured quantity.
wrong: The prefix milli means 10^-3 only when it appears in the numerator.
rows.explanation: Prefixes represent powers of ten and must be applied to the whole measured quantity.

rows.label: significant figures
rows.correct: Significant figures are the reliably known digits plus the first uncertain digit in a measured value.
wrong: All zeros written in a measured number are automatically insignificant.
rows.explanation: Significant figures are the reliably known digits plus the first uncertain digit in a measured value.

rows.label: rounding rules
rows.correct: When rounding, the first discarded digit determines whether the retained last digit changes.
wrong: Every discarded digit causes the retained digit to increase by one.
rows.explanation: When rounding, the first discarded digit determines whether the retained last digit changes.

rows.label: precision versus accuracy
rows.correct: Precision describes repeatability or resolution, while accuracy describes closeness to the accepted value.
wrong: A highly precise measurement must always be accurate.
rows.explanation: Precision describes repeatability or resolution, while accuracy describes closeness to the accepted value.

rows.label: absolute and relative uncertainty
rows.correct: Relative uncertainty is absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value.
wrong: Relative uncertainty carries the same physical unit as the measured quantity.
rows.explanation: Relative uncertainty is absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value.

rows.label: percentage uncertainty
rows.correct: Percentage uncertainty equals one hundred times the relative uncertainty.
wrong: Percentage uncertainty is found by multiplying absolute uncertainty directly by 100.
rows.explanation: Percentage uncertainty equals one hundred times the relative uncertainty.

rows.label: dimensions of a quantity
rows.correct: Dimensions show how a physical quantity depends on base quantities such as mass, length and time.
wrong: Dimensions specify the numerical magnitude of a physical quantity.
rows.explanation: Dimensions show how a physical quantity depends on base quantities such as mass, length and time.

rows.label: dimensionless quantities
rows.correct: A dimensionless quantity can have a numerical value and may sometimes be expressed using a named angular unit.
wrong: Every dimensionless quantity must have numerical value one.
rows.explanation: A dimensionless quantity can have a numerical value and may sometimes be expressed using a named angular unit.

rows.label: same dimensions, different quantities
rows.correct: Distinct physical quantities can share a dimensional formula even though their meanings and units names differ.
wrong: Quantities with the same dimensions are necessarily physically identical.
rows.explanation: Distinct physical quantities can share a dimensional formula even though their meanings and units names differ.

rows.label: dimensions of force
rows.correct: From F = ma, force has dimensions [M L T^-2].
wrong: Force has dimensions [M L^2 T^-2], the dimensions of energy.
rows.explanation: From F = ma, force has dimensions [M L T^-2].

rows.label: dimensions of energy
rows.correct: Work or energy has dimensions [M L^2 T^-2].
wrong: Energy has the same dimensions as power.
rows.explanation: Work or energy has dimensions [M L^2 T^-2].

rows.label: principle of dimensional homogeneity
rows.correct: All additive terms in a physically meaningful equation must have the same dimensions.
wrong: Numerical equality alone guarantees that an equation is dimensionally valid.
rows.explanation: All additive terms in a physically meaningful equation must have the same dimensions.

rows.label: limits of dimensional analysis
rows.correct: Dimensional analysis cannot determine dimensionless numerical constants or distinguish all quantities having the same dimensions.
wrong: Dimensional analysis determines every trigonometric dependence and numerical coefficient.
rows.explanation: Dimensional analysis cannot determine dimensionless numerical constants or distinguish all quantities having the same dimensions.

rows.label: dimensionless arguments
rows.correct: The argument of an exponential, logarithm or trigonometric function must be dimensionless.
wrong: A sine function can accept a dimensional length directly.
rows.explanation: The argument of an exponential, logarithm or trigonometric function must be dimensionless.

rows.label: change of unit numerical value
rows.correct: For fixed quantity Q = n u, numerical value n varies inversely with the chosen unit u.
wrong: Choosing a smaller unit produces a smaller numerical value.
rows.explanation: For fixed quantity Q = n u, numerical value n varies inversely with the chosen unit u.

rows.label: dimensional power-law inference
rows.correct: Powers in a product relation can be found by equating base-dimension exponents.
wrong: Dimensional analysis can fix an arbitrary additive constant.
rows.explanation: Powers in a product relation can be found by equating base-dimension exponents.

rows.label: point-object approximation
rows.correct: An object can be treated as a point when its size is negligible compared with the distance scale of its motion.
wrong: Every moving body must be treated as a point regardless of the problem scale.
rows.explanation: An object can be treated as a point when its size is negligible compared with the distance scale of its motion.

rows.label: displacement
rows.correct: Displacement is the signed change in position and depends only on the initial and final positions.
wrong: Distance travelled and magnitude of displacement are always equal.
rows.explanation: Displacement is the signed change in position and depends only on the initial and final positions.

rows.label: average speed versus average velocity
rows.correct: Average speed uses total distance, while average velocity uses displacement over the same time interval.
wrong: Average speed can be negative when motion is toward the negative x-direction.
rows.explanation: Average speed uses total distance, while average velocity uses displacement over the same time interval.

rows.label: average velocity
rows.correct: Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time.
wrong: Average velocity is always total path length divided by time.
rows.explanation: Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time.

rows.label: average speed
rows.correct: Average speed equals total distance divided by total time and is non-negative.
wrong: Average speed is the arithmetic mean of two speeds in every journey.
rows.explanation: Average speed equals total distance divided by total time and is non-negative.

rows.label: instantaneous velocity
rows.correct: Instantaneous velocity is the limiting value of average velocity as the time interval approaches zero.
wrong: Instantaneous velocity requires a finite one-second interval.
rows.explanation: Instantaneous velocity is the limiting value of average velocity as the time interval approaches zero.

rows.label: slope of an x-t graph
rows.correct: The slope of a position-time graph gives velocity; a steeper signed slope means a larger velocity magnitude.
wrong: The area under a position-time graph gives displacement.
rows.explanation: The slope of a position-time graph gives velocity; a steeper signed slope means a larger velocity magnitude.

rows.label: turning point in one-dimensional motion
rows.correct: At a smooth turning point of x(t), instantaneous velocity is zero and changes sign.
wrong: At every turning point acceleration must also be zero.
rows.explanation: At a smooth turning point of x(t), instantaneous velocity is zero and changes sign.

rows.label: velocity from linear position law
rows.correct: For x = x0 + vt, the coefficient of t is the constant velocity.
wrong: The intercept of an x-t graph is its velocity.
rows.explanation: For x = x0 + vt, the coefficient of t is the constant velocity.

rows.label: instantaneous velocity from quadratic x(t)
rows.correct: For x = at^2 + bt + c, velocity is 2at+b.
wrong: Velocity equals x/t even when x(t) is nonlinear.
rows.explanation: For x = at^2 + bt + c, velocity is 2at+b.

rows.label: acceleration
rows.correct: Acceleration is the time rate of change of velocity and can be nonzero even when speed is momentarily zero.
wrong: Acceleration always points in the direction of motion.
rows.explanation: Acceleration is the time rate of change of velocity and can be nonzero even when speed is momentarily zero.

rows.label: slope and area of a v-t graph
rows.correct: The slope of a velocity-time graph is acceleration and its signed area is displacement.
wrong: The height of a velocity-time graph directly gives acceleration.
rows.explanation: The slope of a velocity-time graph is acceleration and its signed area is displacement.

rows.label: speeding up and slowing down
rows.correct: Speed increases when velocity and acceleration have the same sign and decreases when their signs differ.
wrong: Negative acceleration always means the object is slowing down.
rows.explanation: Speed increases when velocity and acceleration have the same sign and decreases when their signs differ.

rows.label: average acceleration
rows.correct: Average acceleration is change in velocity divided by elapsed time.
wrong: Acceleration is change in position divided by time.
rows.explanation: Average acceleration is change in velocity divided by elapsed time.

rows.label: displacement from constant-acceleration v-t graph
rows.correct: For linearly changing velocity, displacement equals average velocity times time.
wrong: Displacement equals final velocity times time for every accelerated motion.
rows.explanation: For linearly changing velocity, displacement equals average velocity times time.

rows.label: kinematic equations
rows.correct: The standard equations v=u+at, x=ut+(1/2)at^2 and v^2=u^2+2ax require constant acceleration.
wrong: The constant-acceleration equations apply unchanged to arbitrary acceleration.
rows.explanation: The standard equations v=u+at, x=ut+(1/2)at^2 and v^2=u^2+2ax require constant acceleration.

rows.label: free fall sign convention
rows.correct: In free fall near Earth, acceleration has magnitude g downward; its algebraic sign follows the chosen positive axis.
wrong: The value of g changes sign physically when an object moves upward.
rows.explanation: In free fall near Earth, acceleration has magnitude g downward; its algebraic sign follows the chosen positive axis.

rows.label: relative velocity in one dimension
rows.correct: Velocity of A relative to B is vA-vB in a common reference frame.
wrong: Relative speed of two bodies is always the sum of their speeds.
rows.explanation: Velocity of A relative to B is vA-vB in a common reference frame.

rows.label: uniformly accelerated displacement
rows.correct: Displacement under constant acceleration is ut+(1/2)at^2.
wrong: The term (1/2)at^2 may be omitted whenever initial velocity is nonzero.
rows.explanation: Displacement under constant acceleration is ut+(1/2)at^2.

rows.label: relative velocity
rows.correct: Relative velocity is obtained by vector subtraction; in one dimension signs carry the direction.
wrong: Speeds can be subtracted without first assigning directions.
rows.explanation: Relative velocity is obtained by vector subtraction; in one dimension signs carry the direction.

rows.label: scalar and vector quantities
rows.correct: A vector has both magnitude and direction and obeys vector addition; a scalar has magnitude only.
wrong: Every quantity with a positive magnitude is a scalar.
rows.explanation: A vector has both magnitude and direction and obeys vector addition; a scalar has magnitude only.

rows.label: equality and negative of vectors
rows.correct: Equal vectors have the same magnitude and direction independent of their positions; a negative vector reverses direction.
wrong: Vectors are equal only when drawn from the same initial point.
rows.explanation: Equal vectors have the same magnitude and direction independent of their positions; a negative vector reverses direction.

rows.label: triangle and parallelogram laws
rows.correct: Vector addition can be performed head-to-tail or by the parallelogram diagonal.
wrong: Vector addition is performed by simply adding magnitudes in all cases.
rows.explanation: Vector addition can be performed head-to-tail or by the parallelogram diagonal.

rows.label: magnitude of perpendicular resultant
rows.correct: For perpendicular components Ax and Ay, magnitude is sqrt(Ax^2+Ay^2).
wrong: The magnitude is always Ax+Ay.
rows.explanation: For perpendicular components Ax and Ay, magnitude is sqrt(Ax^2+Ay^2).

rows.label: resultant of two vectors
rows.correct: For vectors A and B separated by angle theta, R^2=A^2+B^2+2AB cos theta.
wrong: The resultant magnitude is independent of the angle between vectors.
rows.explanation: For vectors A and B separated by angle theta, R^2=A^2+B^2+2AB cos theta.

rows.label: resolution of a vector
rows.correct: Resolving a vector expresses it as the sum of components along chosen axes.
wrong: A vector has only one possible set of components independent of axes.
rows.explanation: Resolving a vector expresses it as the sum of components along chosen axes.

rows.label: unit vectors
rows.correct: Unit vectors have magnitude one and specify direction; i-hat and j-hat represent Cartesian x and y directions.
wrong: A unit vector must be dimensionless in every use and cannot multiply a dimensional component.
rows.explanation: Unit vectors have magnitude one and specify direction; i-hat and j-hat represent Cartesian x and y directions.

rows.label: component signs and quadrant
rows.correct: The signs of Cartesian components depend on the vector quadrant and chosen positive axes.
wrong: Both components of any vector magnitude are positive.
rows.explanation: The signs of Cartesian components depend on the vector quadrant and chosen positive axes.

rows.label: Cartesian components
rows.correct: A vector A at angle theta from +x has Ax=A cos theta and Ay=A sin theta.
wrong: The x-component is always A sin theta regardless of angle definition.
rows.explanation: A vector A at angle theta from +x has Ax=A cos theta and Ay=A sin theta.

rows.label: direction from components
rows.correct: For a vector with components Ax and Ay, tan theta=Ay/Ax with quadrant correction.
wrong: The ratio Ax/Ay always gives the angle from +x.
rows.explanation: For a vector with components Ax and Ay, tan theta=Ay/Ax with quadrant correction.

rows.label: vector kinematics
rows.correct: Position, velocity and acceleration in a plane are vectors whose Cartesian components can be analysed independently.
wrong: Acceleration in x necessarily changes the y-component of velocity.
rows.explanation: Position, velocity and acceleration in a plane are vectors whose Cartesian components can be analysed independently.

rows.label: constant vector acceleration
rows.correct: With constant acceleration, vector equations have the same form as one-dimensional equations applied componentwise.
wrong: Constant acceleration requires constant speed.
rows.explanation: With constant acceleration, vector equations have the same form as one-dimensional equations applied componentwise.

rows.label: trajectory from components
rows.correct: A trajectory is obtained by eliminating time between component position equations.
wrong: The trajectory equation always contains time explicitly.
rows.explanation: A trajectory is obtained by eliminating time between component position equations.

rows.label: two-dimensional velocity magnitude
rows.correct: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector.
wrong: Speed equals vx+vy even for perpendicular components.
rows.explanation: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector.

rows.label: constant-acceleration component displacement
rows.correct: Each Cartesian displacement follows Delta x=ux t+(1/2)ax t^2 and similarly for y.
wrong: The same scalar acceleration must be inserted in both components.
rows.explanation: Each Cartesian displacement follows Delta x=ux t+(1/2)ax t^2 and similarly for y.

rows.label: projectile independence
rows.correct: Ignoring air resistance, horizontal projectile velocity is constant while vertical acceleration is g downward.
wrong: Gravity reduces horizontal velocity at the same rate as vertical velocity.
rows.explanation: Ignoring air resistance, horizontal projectile velocity is constant while vertical acceleration is g downward.

rows.label: projectile symmetry
rows.correct: For launch and landing at the same level, ascent and descent times are equal and horizontal speeds match.
wrong: At the highest point both horizontal and vertical velocity components are zero.
rows.explanation: For launch and landing at the same level, ascent and descent times are equal and horizontal speeds match.

rows.label: uniform circular motion acceleration
rows.correct: Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity and centripetal acceleration v^2/r toward the centre.
wrong: Zero change in speed means zero acceleration.
rows.explanation: Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity and centripetal acceleration v^2/r toward the centre.

rows.label: projectile range
rows.correct: For equal launch and landing levels, range is u^2 sin(2theta)/g.
wrong: Range is u^2 sin(theta)/g.
rows.explanation: For equal launch and landing levels, range is u^2 sin(2theta)/g.

rows.label: centripetal acceleration
rows.correct: Centripetal acceleration magnitude is v^2/r or omega^2 r.
wrong: Centripetal acceleration is v/r^2.
rows.explanation: Centripetal acceleration magnitude is v^2/r or omega^2 r.

rows.label: Aristotle fallacy
rows.correct: Continuous force is not required to maintain uniform velocity when net external force is zero.
wrong: A moving object necessarily stops because motion itself consumes force.
rows.explanation: Continuous force is not required to maintain uniform velocity when net external force is zero.

rows.label: inertia
rows.correct: Inertia is the tendency to resist a change in velocity and is measured by mass.
wrong: Inertia is a force that pushes a body forward.
rows.explanation: Inertia is the tendency to resist a change in velocity and is measured by mass.

rows.label: Newton first law
rows.correct: A body remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by a net external force.
wrong: Zero net force implies the body must be at rest.
rows.explanation: A body remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by a net external force.

rows.label: net force in uniform motion
rows.correct: Uniform straight-line motion has zero acceleration and therefore zero net force.
wrong: A constant velocity requires a constant nonzero net force.
rows.explanation: Uniform straight-line motion has zero acceleration and therefore zero net force.

rows.label: inertia and mass comparison
rows.correct: For the same force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.
wrong: For the same force, heavier bodies have greater acceleration.
rows.explanation: For the same force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.

rows.label: momentum
rows.correct: Linear momentum is the vector product mv and has the direction of velocity.
wrong: Momentum is a scalar equal to mass times speed only.
rows.explanation: Linear momentum is the vector product mv and has the direction of velocity.

rows.label: Newton second law
rows.correct: Net external force equals the time rate of change of momentum; for constant mass it becomes ma.
wrong: The largest individual force always equals ma even when other forces act.
rows.explanation: Net external force equals the time rate of change of momentum; for constant mass it becomes ma.

rows.label: impulse
rows.correct: Impulse is the time integral of force and equals the change in momentum.
wrong: Impulse equals force divided by contact time.
rows.explanation: Impulse is the time integral of force and equals the change in momentum.

rows.label: constant-mass net force
rows.correct: For constant mass, net force is mass times acceleration.
wrong: The vector net force can be found using speed alone.
rows.explanation: For constant mass, net force is mass times acceleration.

rows.label: average impulsive force
rows.correct: Average force equals momentum change divided by contact time.
wrong: A longer collision time increases average force for the same momentum change.
rows.explanation: Average force equals momentum change divided by contact time.

rows.label: Newton third-law pair
rows.correct: Action and reaction are equal and opposite forces of the same interaction acting on different bodies.
wrong: Third-law forces cancel because they act on the same body.
rows.explanation: Action and reaction are equal and opposite forces of the same interaction acting on different bodies.

rows.label: momentum conservation
rows.correct: Total momentum of a system is constant when net external impulse is zero.
wrong: Internal forces can change total momentum of an isolated system.
rows.explanation: Total momentum of a system is constant when net external impulse is zero.

rows.label: particle equilibrium
rows.correct: A particle is in translational equilibrium when the vector sum of forces is zero.
wrong: Equilibrium requires that no forces act on the particle.
rows.explanation: A particle is in translational equilibrium when the vector sum of forces is zero.

rows.label: one-dimensional recoil
rows.correct: For an initially stationary isolated two-body system, m1v1+m2v2=0.
wrong: Both recoil velocities point in the same direction.
rows.explanation: For an initially stationary isolated two-body system, m1v1+m2v2=0.

rows.label: two-force equilibrium
rows.correct: Two forces alone balance only if equal, opposite and collinear.
wrong: Equal magnitudes guarantee equilibrium regardless of directions.
rows.explanation: Two forces alone balance only if equal, opposite and collinear.

rows.label: normal reaction
rows.correct: The normal force is perpendicular to the contact surface and need not equal weight.
wrong: The normal force on every body always equals mg.
rows.explanation: The normal force is perpendicular to the contact surface and need not equal weight.

rows.label: static and kinetic friction
rows.correct: Static friction adjusts up to its limiting value, while kinetic friction acts during slipping.
wrong: Static friction is always equal to mu_s N even below impending motion.
rows.explanation: Static friction adjusts up to its limiting value, while kinetic friction acts during slipping.

rows.label: free-body diagram
rows.correct: A free-body diagram contains only forces acting on the selected body, with interactions represented once.
wrong: A free-body diagram should include forces exerted by the selected body on other objects.
rows.explanation: A free-body diagram contains only forces acting on the selected body, with interactions represented once.

rows.label: limiting static friction
rows.correct: Maximum static friction is mu_s N.
wrong: Actual static friction is always mu_s N.
rows.explanation: Maximum static friction is mu_s N.

rows.label: centripetal force requirement
rows.correct: The radial net force required for circular motion is mv^2/r toward the centre.
wrong: Centripetal force is an additional force independent of real interactions.
rows.explanation: The radial net force required for circular motion is mv^2/r toward the centre.

rows.label: mechanical work
rows.correct: Work by a constant force is the scalar product F dot displacement and can be positive, negative or zero.
wrong: Any nonzero force necessarily does positive work.
rows.explanation: Work by a constant force is the scalar product F dot displacement and can be positive, negative or zero.

rows.label: kinetic energy
rows.correct: Kinetic energy is (1/2)mv^2, a non-negative scalar that depends on the chosen frame.
wrong: Kinetic energy is a vector in the direction of velocity.
rows.explanation: Kinetic energy is (1/2)mv^2, a non-negative scalar that depends on the chosen frame.

rows.label: work-energy theorem
rows.correct: Net work on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy.
wrong: Work by each individual force always equals the total kinetic-energy change.
rows.explanation: Net work on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy.

rows.label: constant-force work
rows.correct: Work is Fs cos theta for constant force and displacement.
wrong: The angle used is between force and velocity after the motion ends.
rows.explanation: Work is Fs cos theta for constant force and displacement.

rows.label: kinetic energy
rows.correct: Kinetic energy equals one half mass times speed squared.
wrong: Kinetic energy is proportional to speed rather than speed squared.
rows.explanation: Kinetic energy equals one half mass times speed squared.

rows.label: work by variable force
rows.correct: Work by a variable one-dimensional force is the definite integral of F(x) dx and the signed area under the F-x graph.
wrong: The slope of an F-x graph gives work.
rows.explanation: Work by a variable one-dimensional force is the definite integral of F(x) dx and the signed area under the F-x graph.

rows.label: negative net work
rows.correct: Negative net work reduces kinetic energy but does not by itself require displacement to be negative.
wrong: Negative work means the object must move in the negative coordinate direction.
rows.explanation: Negative net work reduces kinetic energy but does not by itself require displacement to be negative.

rows.label: path dependence of work
rows.correct: Work by a general force may depend on path, while net-work change in kinetic energy depends only on initial and final speeds.
wrong: Work by every force depends only on endpoints.
rows.explanation: Work by a general force may depend on path, while net-work change in kinetic energy depends only on initial and final speeds.

rows.label: work from a linear F-x graph
rows.correct: For force increasing linearly from zero to F over distance x, work is the triangular area Fx/2.
wrong: Work equals the final force times distance without the one-half factor.
rows.explanation: For force increasing linearly from zero to F over distance x, work is the triangular area Fx/2.

rows.label: speed from net work
rows.correct: Using Wnet=Delta K, final speed follows from Kf=Ki+Wnet.
wrong: Net work should be added directly to speed.
rows.explanation: Using Wnet=Delta K, final speed follows from Kf=Ki+Wnet.

rows.label: conservative force
rows.correct: For a conservative force, work between two points is path independent and equals minus the change in potential energy.
wrong: A conservative force always does positive work.
rows.explanation: For a conservative force, work between two points is path independent and equals minus the change in potential energy.

rows.label: potential-energy reference
rows.correct: Only potential-energy differences affect mechanics; the zero level may be chosen conveniently.
wrong: Potential energy has one absolute zero fixed for every problem.
rows.explanation: Only potential-energy differences affect mechanics; the zero level may be chosen conveniently.

rows.label: mechanical-energy conservation
rows.correct: When only conservative forces do work, K+U remains constant.
wrong: Mechanical energy remains constant even with dissipative friction and no other energy transfer.
rows.explanation: When only conservative forces do work, K+U remains constant.

rows.label: near-Earth gravitational potential energy
rows.correct: Near Earth, a height change h changes gravitational potential energy by mgh.
wrong: Gravitational potential energy change depends on path length.
rows.explanation: Near Earth, a height change h changes gravitational potential energy by mgh.

rows.label: speed from falling height
rows.correct: With negligible resistance, loss of mgh becomes kinetic energy.
wrong: Heavier bodies fall faster because they lose more potential energy.
rows.explanation: With negligible resistance, loss of mgh becomes kinetic energy.

rows.label: spring potential energy
rows.correct: An ideal spring stores potential energy (1/2)kx^2 relative to its natural length.
wrong: Spring potential energy is kx and can be negative for compression.
rows.explanation: An ideal spring stores potential energy (1/2)kx^2 relative to its natural length.

rows.label: power
rows.correct: Instantaneous power is the rate of doing work and equals F dot v for a particle.
wrong: High power necessarily means a large total amount of work.
rows.explanation: Instantaneous power is the rate of doing work and equals F dot v for a particle.

rows.label: elastic and inelastic collision
rows.correct: Momentum is conserved in an isolated collision; kinetic energy is additionally conserved only in an elastic collision.
wrong: Kinetic energy is conserved in every isolated collision.
rows.explanation: Momentum is conserved in an isolated collision; kinetic energy is additionally conserved only in an elastic collision.

rows.label: spring energy
rows.correct: Spring energy is one half kx squared.
wrong: For a fixed spring, stored energy is directly proportional to extension.
rows.explanation: Spring energy is one half kx squared.

rows.label: average power
rows.correct: Average power equals work divided by elapsed time.
wrong: Power equals work multiplied by time.
rows.explanation: Average power equals work divided by elapsed time.

chapters.name: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

rows.label: centre of mass
rows.correct: The centre of mass is the mass-weighted average position and can lie outside the material of a body.
wrong: The centre of mass must always lie inside matter.
rows.explanation: The centre of mass is the mass-weighted average position and can lie outside the material of a body.

rows.label: motion of centre of mass
rows.correct: Total external force equals total mass times centre-of-mass acceleration.
wrong: Internal forces can accelerate the centre of mass of an isolated system.
rows.explanation: Total external force equals total mass times centre-of-mass acceleration.

rows.label: system momentum
rows.correct: Total linear momentum equals total mass times centre-of-mass velocity.
wrong: Centre-of-mass velocity is the unweighted average of all particle velocities.
rows.explanation: Total linear momentum equals total mass times centre-of-mass velocity.

rows.label: two-particle centre of mass
rows.correct: For positions x1 and x2, xcm=(m1x1+m2x2)/(m1+m2).
wrong: The centre of mass is always the midpoint independent of masses.
rows.explanation: For positions x1 and x2, xcm=(m1x1+m2x2)/(m1+m2).

rows.label: centre-of-mass acceleration
rows.correct: Centre-of-mass acceleration is net external force divided by total mass.
wrong: It is determined by the largest internal force.
rows.explanation: Centre-of-mass acceleration is net external force divided by total mass.

rows.label: vector product
rows.correct: The cross product a x b has magnitude ab sin theta and direction from the right-hand rule.
wrong: The cross product is commutative: a x b=b x a.
rows.explanation: The cross product a x b has magnitude ab sin theta and direction from the right-hand rule.

rows.label: angular velocity
rows.correct: For rotation about a fixed axis, angular velocity points along the axis by the right-hand rule.
wrong: Angular velocity points tangentially along particle motion.
rows.explanation: For rotation about a fixed axis, angular velocity points along the axis by the right-hand rule.

rows.label: rotational kinematics analogy
rows.correct: For constant angular acceleration, angular equations mirror linear constant-acceleration equations.
wrong: Angular displacement is always equal to arc length.
rows.explanation: For constant angular acceleration, angular equations mirror linear constant-acceleration equations.

rows.label: linear-angular speed relation
rows.correct: For fixed-axis rotation, tangential speed is omega r.
wrong: Every point of a rigid body has the same tangential speed.
rows.explanation: For fixed-axis rotation, tangential speed is omega r.

rows.label: constant angular acceleration
rows.correct: Angular speed changes as omega=omega0+alpha t for constant alpha.
wrong: Angular speed changes as omega0+alpha t^2.
rows.explanation: Angular speed changes as omega=omega0+alpha t for constant alpha.

rows.label: torque
rows.correct: Torque about an origin is r x F and measures the turning effect of force.
wrong: Torque magnitude is always rF even when force is parallel to r.
rows.explanation: Torque about an origin is r x F and measures the turning effect of force.

rows.label: angular momentum
rows.correct: Particle angular momentum about an origin is r x p and depends on the chosen origin.
wrong: Angular momentum is always parallel to linear momentum.
rows.explanation: Particle angular momentum about an origin is r x p and depends on the chosen origin.

rows.label: rigid-body equilibrium
rows.correct: Complete rigid-body equilibrium requires both zero net force and zero net torque.
wrong: Zero net force alone prevents every kind of rigid-body acceleration.
rows.explanation: Complete rigid-body equilibrium requires both zero net force and zero net torque.

rows.label: torque magnitude
rows.correct: Torque magnitude is rF sin theta.
wrong: Only force magnitude matters, not its line of action.
rows.explanation: Torque magnitude is rF sin theta.

rows.label: angular momentum of perpendicular motion
rows.correct: When r is perpendicular to mv, angular momentum magnitude is mvr.
wrong: Angular momentum magnitude is mv/r.
rows.explanation: When r is perpendicular to mv, angular momentum magnitude is mvr.

rows.label: moment of inertia
rows.correct: Moment of inertia is sum or integral of mass times squared perpendicular distance from the rotation axis.
wrong: Moment of inertia depends only on total mass and never on axis location.
rows.explanation: Moment of inertia is sum or integral of mass times squared perpendicular distance from the rotation axis.

rows.label: parallel and perpendicular axis theorems
rows.correct: The parallel-axis theorem adds Md^2 to the centre-of-mass-axis value; the perpendicular-axis theorem applies to a planar lamina.
wrong: The perpendicular-axis theorem applies to any three-dimensional body.
rows.explanation: The parallel-axis theorem adds Md^2 to the centre-of-mass-axis value; the perpendicular-axis theorem applies to a planar lamina.

rows.label: rotational dynamics
rows.correct: For fixed-axis rotation, net torque equals I alpha and rotational kinetic energy is (1/2)I omega^2.
wrong: A larger moment of inertia gives larger angular acceleration for the same torque.
rows.explanation: For fixed-axis rotation, net torque equals I alpha and rotational kinetic energy is (1/2)I omega^2.

rows.label: fixed-axis angular acceleration
rows.correct: Angular acceleration is net torque divided by moment of inertia.
wrong: Angular acceleration is the product of torque and moment of inertia.
rows.explanation: Angular acceleration is net torque divided by moment of inertia.

rows.label: rotational kinetic energy
rows.correct: Rotational kinetic energy is one half I omega squared.
wrong: Rotational kinetic energy is linear in angular speed.
rows.explanation: Rotational kinetic energy is one half I omega squared.

rows.label: Kepler first law
rows.correct: Each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.
wrong: The Sun lies at the geometric centre of every planetary ellipse.
rows.explanation: Each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.

rows.label: Kepler second and third laws
rows.correct: Equal areas are swept in equal times, and orbital period squared is proportional to semi-major axis cubed for the same central mass.
wrong: A planet moves with constant speed everywhere in an elliptical orbit.
rows.explanation: Equal areas are swept in equal times, and orbital period squared is proportional to semi-major axis cubed for the same central mass.

rows.label: universal gravitation
rows.correct: Two point masses attract along their joining line with force Gm1m2/r^2.
wrong: Gravitational force can be repulsive for opposite signs of mass.
rows.explanation: Two point masses attract along their joining line with force Gm1m2/r^2.

rows.label: Newton gravitational force
rows.correct: Gravitational force follows an inverse-square dependence on separation.
wrong: Gravitational force is proportional to separation squared.
rows.explanation: Gravitational force follows an inverse-square dependence on separation.

rows.label: Kepler third-law ratio
rows.correct: For the same central mass, T^2/a^3 is constant.
wrong: Orbital period is directly proportional to orbital radius.
rows.explanation: For the same central mass, T^2/a^3 is constant.

rows.label: surface gravity
rows.correct: At a spherical planet surface, g=GM/R^2 and is independent of the falling test mass.
wrong: Heavier falling bodies experience a larger gravitational acceleration in vacuum.
rows.explanation: At a spherical planet surface, g=GM/R^2 and is independent of the falling test mass.

rows.label: gravity above and below Earth
rows.correct: Above Earth g decreases approximately as inverse square of distance from the centre; inside a uniform Earth it decreases linearly toward zero at the centre.
wrong: Gravity is greatest at Earth centre because all mass surrounds the object.
rows.explanation: Above Earth g decreases approximately as inverse square of distance from the centre; inside a uniform Earth it decreases linearly toward zero at the centre.

rows.label: inertial and gravitational mass
rows.correct: Equality of inertial and gravitational mass explains the mass-independent free-fall acceleration.
wrong: The gravitational mass cancels only because its value is zero.
rows.explanation: Equality of inertial and gravitational mass explains the mass-independent free-fall acceleration.

rows.label: surface gravitational acceleration
rows.correct: Surface gravity is GM/R squared.
wrong: Surface gravity is GM/R.
rows.explanation: Surface gravity is GM/R squared.

rows.label: gravity at altitude
rows.correct: At altitude h, g_h=g0[R/(R+h)]^2.
wrong: Gravity at altitude falls linearly to zero at h=R.
rows.explanation: At altitude h, g_h=g0[R/(R+h)]^2.

rows.label: gravitational potential energy
rows.correct: With zero at infinity, two separated masses have U=-GMm/r.
wrong: Gravitational potential energy is positive for an attractive bound pair with zero at infinity.
rows.explanation: With zero at infinity, two separated masses have U=-GMm/r.

rows.label: gravitational potential
rows.correct: Potential is potential energy per unit test mass and superposes algebraically.
wrong: Gravitational potential is a vector directed toward mass.
rows.explanation: Potential is potential energy per unit test mass and superposes algebraically.

rows.label: escape speed
rows.correct: Escape speed is the minimum launch speed to reach infinity with zero residual speed when resistance and further propulsion are absent.
wrong: Escape speed depends on the mass of the projectile.
rows.explanation: Escape speed is the minimum launch speed to reach infinity with zero residual speed when resistance and further propulsion are absent.

rows.label: gravitational potential energy
rows.correct: Potential energy of two point masses is -GMm/r with zero at infinity.
wrong: The negative sign means gravitational force does negative work during attraction.
rows.explanation: Potential energy of two point masses is -GMm/r with zero at infinity.

rows.label: escape speed
rows.correct: Surface escape speed is sqrt(2GM/R)=sqrt(2gR).
wrong: Escape speed equals orbital speed at the same radius.
rows.explanation: Surface escape speed is sqrt(2GM/R)=sqrt(2gR).

rows.label: circular satellite orbit
rows.correct: Gravity supplies the centripetal force for a freely orbiting satellite.
wrong: An orbiting satellite has zero acceleration because it feels weightless.
rows.explanation: Gravity supplies the centripetal force for a freely orbiting satellite.

rows.label: geostationary satellite
rows.correct: A geostationary satellite has a circular equatorial orbit, moves west-to-east and has Earths rotational period.
wrong: Any satellite with a 24-hour period is geostationary regardless of orbital plane or direction.
rows.explanation: A geostationary satellite has a circular equatorial orbit, moves west-to-east and has Earths rotational period.

rows.label: orbital energy
rows.correct: For a circular gravitational orbit, K=GMm/(2r), U=-GMm/r and total E=-GMm/(2r).
wrong: A bound circular satellite has positive total mechanical energy.
rows.explanation: For a circular gravitational orbit, K=GMm/(2r), U=-GMm/r and total E=-GMm/(2r).

rows.label: circular orbital speed
rows.correct: Circular orbital speed is sqrt(GM/r).
wrong: Orbital speed increases with orbital radius.
rows.explanation: Circular orbital speed is sqrt(GM/r).

rows.label: circular-orbit total energy
rows.correct: Total energy in a circular orbit is -GMm/(2r).
wrong: Total energy equals potential energy alone.
rows.explanation: Total energy in a circular orbit is -GMm/(2r).

rows.label: elasticity and plasticity
rows.correct: Elasticity is the tendency to regain original size and shape after removal of deforming force; plastic deformation remains.
wrong: A material that undergoes a larger strain is necessarily more elastic.
rows.explanation: Elasticity is the tendency to regain original size and shape after removal of deforming force; plastic deformation remains.

rows.label: stress
rows.correct: Stress is the internal restoring force per unit area and has SI unit pascal.
wrong: Stress is the total external force and therefore has unit newton.
rows.explanation: Stress is the internal restoring force per unit area and has SI unit pascal.

rows.label: strain
rows.correct: Strain is a fractional change in dimension and is dimensionless.
wrong: Longitudinal strain has the unit metre because it contains a length change.
rows.explanation: Strain is a fractional change in dimension and is dimensionless.

rows.label: longitudinal stress
rows.correct: Longitudinal stress is normal force divided by cross-sectional area.
wrong: Using diameter in place of cross-sectional area gives the correct stress.
rows.explanation: Longitudinal stress is normal force divided by cross-sectional area.

rows.label: longitudinal strain
rows.correct: Longitudinal strain is extension divided by original length.
wrong: Strain is extension multiplied by original length.
rows.explanation: Longitudinal strain is extension divided by original length.

rows.label: Hooke law
rows.correct: For sufficiently small deformation, stress is proportional to strain; the proportionality limit must not be ignored.
wrong: Hooke law applies to every deformation up to fracture.
rows.explanation: For sufficiently small deformation, stress is proportional to strain; the proportionality limit must not be ignored.

rows.label: elastic and plastic regions
rows.correct: Below the elastic limit a specimen regains its dimensions; beyond yield it can retain a permanent set.
wrong: The proportional limit, elastic limit and fracture point are always the same.
rows.explanation: Below the elastic limit a specimen regains its dimensions; beyond yield it can retain a permanent set.

rows.label: ductility and brittleness
rows.correct: A ductile material sustains substantial plastic strain before fracture, whereas a brittle material fractures with little plastic deformation.
wrong: A brittle material must have a smaller Young modulus than every ductile material.
rows.explanation: A ductile material sustains substantial plastic strain before fracture, whereas a brittle material fractures with little plastic deformation.

rows.label: modulus from graph slope
rows.correct: In the linear region, the slope of stress versus strain is the elastic modulus.
wrong: The area under a stress-strain graph is the elastic modulus.
rows.explanation: In the linear region, the slope of stress versus strain is the elastic modulus.

rows.label: elastic energy density
rows.correct: For linear elastic loading, energy stored per unit volume is one half stress times strain.
wrong: Elastic energy density equals stress divided by strain.
rows.explanation: For linear elastic loading, energy stored per unit volume is one half stress times strain.

rows.label: Young modulus
rows.correct: Young modulus is longitudinal stress divided by longitudinal strain within the linear elastic range.
wrong: A larger Young modulus means a larger strain for the same stress.
rows.explanation: Young modulus is longitudinal stress divided by longitudinal strain within the linear elastic range.

rows.label: shear modulus
rows.correct: Shear modulus is tangential stress divided by shear strain, with shear strain approximately equal to the small shear angle in radians.
wrong: Shearing stress changes volume without changing shape.
rows.explanation: Shear modulus is tangential stress divided by shear strain, with shear strain approximately equal to the small shear angle in radians.

rows.label: bulk modulus and compressibility
rows.correct: Bulk modulus relates pressure increase to fractional volume decrease, and compressibility is its reciprocal.
wrong: A highly incompressible material has a small bulk modulus.
rows.explanation: Bulk modulus relates pressure increase to fractional volume decrease, and compressibility is its reciprocal.

rows.label: extension using Young modulus
rows.correct: For a uniform wire in the elastic range, extension is FL/(AY).
wrong: Extension is proportional to cross-sectional area and Young modulus.
rows.explanation: For a uniform wire in the elastic range, extension is FL/(AY).

rows.label: volume change using bulk modulus
rows.correct: The magnitude of fractional volume change is pressure increase divided by bulk modulus.
wrong: Volume strain is pressure multiplied by bulk modulus.
rows.explanation: The magnitude of fractional volume change is pressure increase divided by bulk modulus.

rows.label: elastic stiffness of a wire
rows.correct: For the same material and length, axial stiffness YA/L increases with cross-sectional area.
wrong: A thinner wire is stiffer because it experiences greater stress.
rows.explanation: For the same material and length, axial stiffness YA/L increases with cross-sectional area.

rows.label: beam design
rows.correct: An I-shaped cross-section places material away from the neutral region and improves resistance to bending without excessive mass.
wrong: The neutral central material contributes most strongly to bending resistance.
rows.explanation: An I-shaped cross-section places material away from the neutral region and improves resistance to bending without excessive mass.

rows.label: load safety and yield strength
rows.correct: Engineering design keeps working stress safely below yield strength using a factor of safety.
wrong: A structure is safe whenever its working stress is below ultimate fracture stress.
rows.explanation: Engineering design keeps working stress safely below yield strength using a factor of safety.

rows.label: wire stiffness
rows.correct: Axial force constant of a wire is YA/L.
wrong: Wire stiffness is YL/A.
rows.explanation: Axial force constant of a wire is YA/L.

rows.label: safe load
rows.correct: Safe load equals allowable stress times load-bearing area.
wrong: Safe load is allowable stress divided by area.
rows.explanation: Safe load equals allowable stress times load-bearing area.

rows.label: fluid pressure
rows.correct: A fluid at rest exerts pressure normal to a surface, and at the same level in a connected static fluid pressure is the same.
wrong: Static-fluid pressure acts only vertically downward.
rows.explanation: A fluid at rest exerts pressure normal to a surface, and at the same level in a connected static fluid pressure is the same.

rows.label: Pascal law
rows.correct: A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid and container walls.
wrong: A hydraulic machine creates energy because output force exceeds input force.
rows.explanation: A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid and container walls.

rows.label: Archimedes principle
rows.correct: Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid and acts upward through the centre of buoyancy.
wrong: Buoyant force always equals the weight of the immersed object.
rows.explanation: Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid and acts upward through the centre of buoyancy.

rows.label: hydrostatic pressure increase
rows.correct: Pressure increases with depth by rho gh for a uniform incompressible fluid.
wrong: Hydrostatic pressure depends on container shape rather than depth.
rows.explanation: Pressure increases with depth by rho gh for a uniform incompressible fluid.

rows.label: hydraulic force multiplication
rows.correct: Equal transmitted pressure gives F1/A1=F2/A2.
wrong: Equal pressure requires equal forces even for unequal piston areas.
rows.explanation: Equal transmitted pressure gives F1/A1=F2/A2.

rows.label: streamline flow
rows.correct: In steady flow, velocity at a fixed point does not change with time and streamlines do not cross.
wrong: Two streamlines may cross because a fluid particle can have two velocities at one point.
rows.explanation: In steady flow, velocity at a fixed point does not change with time and streamlines do not cross.

rows.label: equation of continuity
rows.correct: For steady incompressible flow, Av is constant along a flow tube by conservation of mass.
wrong: Fluid speed is greatest where pipe area is greatest.
rows.explanation: For steady incompressible flow, Av is constant along a flow tube by conservation of mass.

rows.label: Bernoulli principle
rows.correct: Along a streamline in steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow, P plus rho v squared over two plus rho gy is constant.
wrong: Bernoulli equation applies unchanged across a pump or large viscous loss.
rows.explanation: Along a streamline in steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow, P plus rho v squared over two plus rho gy is constant.

rows.label: continuity speed
rows.correct: For incompressible steady flow, A1v1=A2v2.
wrong: Speed is directly proportional to cross-sectional area.
rows.explanation: For incompressible steady flow, A1v1=A2v2.

rows.label: Torricelli efflux speed
rows.correct: For a small opening at depth h in a large tank, ideal efflux speed is sqrt(2gh).
wrong: Efflux speed is proportional to depth rather than its square root.
rows.explanation: For a small opening at depth h in a large tank, ideal efflux speed is sqrt(2gh).

rows.label: viscosity
rows.correct: Viscosity is internal fluid friction opposing relative motion of adjacent layers.
wrong: Viscosity of a fluid at rest produces a permanent shear strain like a solid.
rows.explanation: Viscosity is internal fluid friction opposing relative motion of adjacent layers.

rows.label: Reynolds number
rows.correct: Reynolds number compares inertial and viscous effects and helps predict streamline or turbulent flow.
wrong: Reynolds number has SI unit pascal second.
rows.explanation: Reynolds number compares inertial and viscous effects and helps predict streamline or turbulent flow.

rows.label: terminal velocity
rows.correct: At terminal speed, viscous drag plus buoyancy balances weight so acceleration becomes zero.
wrong: At terminal speed all forces vanish individually.
rows.explanation: At terminal speed, viscous drag plus buoyancy balances weight so acceleration becomes zero.

rows.label: Stokes drag
rows.correct: For slow motion of a sphere, viscous drag is 6 pi eta r v.
wrong: Stokes drag varies with the square of sphere speed.
rows.explanation: For slow motion of a sphere, viscous drag is 6 pi eta r v.

rows.label: terminal speed of a sphere
rows.correct: Stokes-law terminal speed is 2 r squared (rho_s-rho_f)g divided by 9 eta.
wrong: Terminal speed is directly proportional to radius.
rows.explanation: Stokes-law terminal speed is 2 r squared (rho_s-rho_f)g divided by 9 eta.

rows.label: surface tension and surface energy
rows.correct: Surface tension is force per unit length and numerically equals surface energy per unit area at constant temperature.
wrong: Surface tension acts perpendicular to the liquid surface.
rows.explanation: Surface tension is force per unit length and numerically equals surface energy per unit area at constant temperature.

rows.label: angle of contact
rows.correct: Angle of contact is measured through the liquid and depends on the liquid-solid-medium combination.
wrong: The angle of contact is a property of the liquid alone.
rows.explanation: Angle of contact is measured through the liquid and depends on the liquid-solid-medium combination.

rows.label: capillarity
rows.correct: Capillary rise or depression results from surface tension, wetting and hydrostatic balance.
wrong: A wider capillary produces a larger rise for the same liquid.
rows.explanation: Capillary rise or depression results from surface tension, wetting and hydrostatic balance.

rows.label: excess pressure in a drop
rows.correct: Excess pressure inside a liquid drop is 2S/r, while a soap bubble has two surfaces and 4S/r.
wrong: A liquid drop and soap bubble of equal radius have equal excess pressure.
rows.explanation: Excess pressure inside a liquid drop is 2S/r, while a soap bubble has two surfaces and 4S/r.

rows.label: capillary rise
rows.correct: For a tube of radius r, h=2S cos theta/(rho g r).
wrong: Capillary rise is directly proportional to tube radius.
rows.explanation: For a tube of radius r, h=2S cos theta/(rho g r).

rows.label: heat and temperature
rows.correct: Temperature determines the direction of spontaneous heat flow; heat is energy transferred because of temperature difference.
wrong: A body contains a definite amount of heat as a state variable.
rows.explanation: Temperature determines the direction of spontaneous heat flow; heat is energy transferred because of temperature difference.

rows.label: thermometric property
rows.correct: A thermometer uses a reproducible property that varies with temperature and is calibrated at fixed points.
wrong: Every thermometric property varies identically at all temperatures.
rows.explanation: A thermometer uses a reproducible property that varies with temperature and is calibrated at fixed points.

rows.label: absolute temperature
rows.correct: Kelvin temperature has the same interval size as Celsius and is related by T=tC+273.15.
wrong: A temperature of 0 degree Celsius means zero molecular activity.
rows.explanation: Kelvin temperature has the same interval size as Celsius and is related by T=tC+273.15.

rows.label: Celsius-Fahrenheit conversion
rows.correct: Celsius and Fahrenheit scales satisfy tF=(9/5)tC+32.
wrong: A Celsius temperature is converted to Fahrenheit by adding 273.15.
rows.explanation: Celsius and Fahrenheit scales satisfy tF=(9/5)tC+32.

rows.label: constant-volume gas thermometer
rows.correct: At fixed amount and volume of an ideal gas, absolute temperature is proportional to pressure.
wrong: At fixed volume, absolute temperature is inversely proportional to gas pressure.
rows.explanation: At fixed amount and volume of an ideal gas, absolute temperature is proportional to pressure.

rows.label: linear expansion
rows.correct: For a small temperature change, fractional length change is alpha times temperature change.
wrong: A hole in a uniformly heated sheet contracts because material expands inward.
rows.explanation: For a small temperature change, fractional length change is alpha times temperature change.

rows.label: area and volume expansion
rows.correct: For an isotropic solid, area and volume expansion coefficients are approximately 2 alpha and 3 alpha.
wrong: The volume expansion coefficient of an isotropic solid equals its linear coefficient.
rows.explanation: For an isotropic solid, area and volume expansion coefficients are approximately 2 alpha and 3 alpha.

rows.label: anomalous expansion of water
rows.correct: Water has maximum density near 4 degree Celsius and expands when cooled from 4 degree Celsius to 0 degree Celsius.
wrong: Water contracts continuously on cooling down to freezing.
rows.explanation: Water has maximum density near 4 degree Celsius and expands when cooled from 4 degree Celsius to 0 degree Celsius.

rows.label: linear thermal expansion
rows.correct: Length change is alpha L Delta T for small expansion.
wrong: Length change is independent of original length.
rows.explanation: Length change is alpha L Delta T for small expansion.

rows.label: apparent liquid expansion
rows.correct: Apparent volume expansion of a liquid in a vessel is approximately (gamma_liquid-gamma_vessel)V Delta T.
wrong: Container expansion should be added to obtain apparent expansion.
rows.explanation: Apparent volume expansion of a liquid in a vessel is approximately (gamma_liquid-gamma_vessel)V Delta T.

rows.label: specific heat capacity
rows.correct: Specific heat capacity is heat required per unit mass per unit temperature rise.
wrong: A substance with high specific heat warms more for the same heat per unit mass.
rows.explanation: Specific heat capacity is heat required per unit mass per unit temperature rise.

rows.label: calorimetry principle
rows.correct: In an isolated calorimeter, heat lost by hotter bodies equals heat gained by colder bodies until equilibrium.
wrong: Final equilibrium temperature can lie outside the initial temperature range without a phase change.
rows.explanation: In an isolated calorimeter, heat lost by hotter bodies equals heat gained by colder bodies until equilibrium.

rows.label: latent heat
rows.correct: During an ideal phase change at fixed pressure, supplied heat changes phase while temperature remains constant.
wrong: Latent heat necessarily raises temperature throughout melting or boiling.
rows.explanation: During an ideal phase change at fixed pressure, supplied heat changes phase while temperature remains constant.

rows.label: sensible heat
rows.correct: Without phase change, heat is mc Delta T.
wrong: Heat capacity equals specific heat divided by mass.
rows.explanation: Without phase change, heat is mc Delta T.

rows.label: latent heat transfer
rows.correct: Heat for a phase change is mL.
wrong: Latent heat transfer is inversely proportional to mass.
rows.explanation: Heat for a phase change is mL.

rows.label: conduction
rows.correct: Conduction transfers energy through microscopic interactions without bulk transport of matter.
wrong: Good thermal insulators must have high thermal conductivity.
rows.explanation: Conduction transfers energy through microscopic interactions without bulk transport of matter.

rows.label: convection and radiation
rows.correct: Convection involves bulk fluid motion, while thermal radiation can cross vacuum.
wrong: Convection is the dominant heat-transfer mode through empty space.
rows.explanation: Convection involves bulk fluid motion, while thermal radiation can cross vacuum.

rows.label: Newton law of cooling
rows.correct: For modest temperature differences under fixed conditions, cooling rate is proportional to excess temperature above surroundings.
wrong: A cooling body loses equal temperature in equal times at every temperature.
rows.explanation: For modest temperature differences under fixed conditions, cooling rate is proportional to excess temperature above surroundings.

rows.label: steady conduction rate
rows.correct: For a uniform slab, heat current is KA Delta T/L.
wrong: Increasing slab thickness increases heat current.
rows.explanation: For a uniform slab, heat current is KA Delta T/L.

rows.label: radiated power
rows.correct: Net radiative power is epsilon sigma A(T fourth-Ts fourth).
wrong: Radiative power depends linearly on absolute temperature.
rows.explanation: Net radiative power is epsilon sigma A(T fourth-Ts fourth).

rows.label: thermal equilibrium
rows.correct: Two systems in thermal equilibrium have no net heat transfer when placed in thermal contact.
wrong: Thermal equilibrium requires equal internal energies.
rows.explanation: Two systems in thermal equilibrium have no net heat transfer when placed in thermal contact.

rows.label: zeroth law
rows.correct: If two systems are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
wrong: The zeroth law is a statement that internal energy is conserved.
rows.explanation: If two systems are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

rows.label: state variables and equation of state
rows.correct: Pressure, volume and temperature describe equilibrium states; heat and work depend on the path.
wrong: Heat supplied is a state variable fixed only by initial and final states.
rows.explanation: Pressure, volume and temperature describe equilibrium states; heat and work depend on the path.

rows.label: ideal gas equation of state
rows.correct: For an ideal gas, PV=nRT.
wrong: The product PV is constant for every process regardless of temperature.
rows.explanation: For an ideal gas, PV=nRT.

rows.label: state change at fixed amount
rows.correct: For a fixed ideal-gas sample, P1V1/T1=P2V2/T2.
wrong: Celsius temperatures may be used directly in gas-law ratios.
rows.explanation: For a fixed ideal-gas sample, P1V1/T1=P2V2/T2.

rows.label: internal energy
rows.correct: Internal energy is microscopic kinetic plus intermolecular potential energy and excludes overall centre-of-mass kinetic energy.
wrong: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends on its container volume alone.
rows.explanation: Internal energy is microscopic kinetic plus intermolecular potential energy and excludes overall centre-of-mass kinetic energy.

rows.label: heat and work sign convention
rows.correct: In NCERT convention Q is positive into the system and W is positive when done by the system.
wrong: Compression work done on a gas is positive work by the gas.
rows.explanation: In NCERT convention Q is positive into the system and W is positive when done by the system.

rows.label: first law of thermodynamics
rows.correct: Energy conservation gives Delta Q=Delta U+Delta W when W is work done by the system.
wrong: In every process heat supplied equals work done because internal energy never changes.
rows.explanation: Energy conservation gives Delta Q=Delta U+Delta W when W is work done by the system.

rows.label: first-law energy change
rows.correct: With NCERT signs, internal-energy change is Q-W.
wrong: Work done by the system must be added to heat to find internal-energy gain.
rows.explanation: With NCERT signs, internal-energy change is Q-W.

rows.label: constant-pressure work
rows.correct: For quasistatic expansion at constant pressure, work by the gas is P Delta V.
wrong: P-V graph slope equals work done.
rows.explanation: For quasistatic expansion at constant pressure, work by the gas is P Delta V.

rows.label: isothermal process
rows.correct: For an ideal gas in an isothermal process, internal energy change is zero and heat absorbed equals work done.
wrong: Isothermal expansion has no heat transfer.
rows.explanation: For an ideal gas in an isothermal process, internal energy change is zero and heat absorbed equals work done.

rows.label: adiabatic, isochoric and isobaric processes
rows.correct: Adiabatic means Q=0, isochoric means W=0, and isobaric means pressure is constant.
wrong: Adiabatic and isothermal processes are identical because both keep temperature constant.
rows.explanation: Adiabatic means Q=0, isochoric means W=0, and isobaric means pressure is constant.

rows.label: cyclic process
rows.correct: Over a complete cycle the state returns to its start so Delta U=0, while net work is the signed enclosed P-V area.
wrong: Net work over every cycle is zero because the final state equals the initial state.
rows.explanation: Over a complete cycle the state returns to its start so Delta U=0, while net work is the signed enclosed P-V area.

rows.label: isothermal ideal-gas work
rows.correct: Reversible isothermal work is nRT ln(V2/V1).
wrong: Isothermal work is simply P1(V2-V1) despite changing pressure.
rows.explanation: Reversible isothermal work is nRT ln(V2/V1).

rows.label: adiabatic work
rows.correct: For an ideal gas, adiabatic work by the gas is nR(T1-T2)/(gamma-1).
wrong: During adiabatic expansion temperature must remain unchanged.
rows.explanation: For an ideal gas, adiabatic work by the gas is nR(T1-T2)/(gamma-1).

rows.label: second law statements
rows.correct: Kelvin-Planck forbids complete cyclic conversion of heat from one reservoir into work; Clausius forbids unaided heat flow cold to hot.
wrong: The first law alone sets the maximum possible heat-engine efficiency.
rows.explanation: Kelvin-Planck forbids complete cyclic conversion of heat from one reservoir into work; Clausius forbids unaided heat flow cold to hot.

rows.label: reversible and irreversible processes
rows.correct: A reversible process is an ideal limit with no dissipative effects and restores both system and surroundings when reversed.
wrong: Every quasistatic process is reversible even with friction.
rows.explanation: A reversible process is an ideal limit with no dissipative effects and restores both system and surroundings when reversed.

rows.label: Carnot theorem
rows.correct: No engine between two given reservoir temperatures is more efficient than a reversible Carnot engine.
wrong: Carnot efficiency depends on the working substance and engine size.
rows.explanation: No engine between two given reservoir temperatures is more efficient than a reversible Carnot engine.

rows.label: Carnot efficiency
rows.correct: Carnot efficiency is 1-Tc/Th with absolute temperatures.
wrong: Celsius temperatures can be inserted directly into the Carnot ratio.
rows.explanation: Carnot efficiency is 1-Tc/Th with absolute temperatures.

rows.label: refrigerator coefficient of performance
rows.correct: For a Carnot refrigerator, COP is Tc/(Th-Tc).
wrong: Refrigerator COP must be less than one like engine efficiency.
rows.explanation: For a Carnot refrigerator, COP is Tc/(Th-Tc).

rows.label: molecular nature of matter
rows.correct: Macroscopic matter consists of atoms or molecules whose microscopic motion and interactions underlie thermal behaviour.
wrong: Gas molecules remain stationary between collisions.
rows.explanation: Macroscopic matter consists of atoms or molecules whose microscopic motion and interactions underlie thermal behaviour.

rows.label: ideal gas approximation
rows.correct: Real gases approach ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature where molecular size and attractions are less important.
wrong: Real gases are most ideal at high pressure and low temperature.
rows.explanation: Real gases approach ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature where molecular size and attractions are less important.

rows.label: Avogadro and Boltzmann constants
rows.correct: One mole contains Avogadro number of entities and R=NA kB.
wrong: Boltzmann constant is the gas constant per kilogram.
rows.explanation: One mole contains Avogadro number of entities and R=NA kB.

rows.label: ideal-gas pressure
rows.correct: Ideal gas pressure is nRT/V.
wrong: Pressure is proportional to volume at fixed n and T.
rows.explanation: Ideal gas pressure is nRT/V.

rows.label: number density
rows.correct: Number density is number of molecules divided by volume.
wrong: Number density equals molecular mass times volume.
rows.explanation: Number density is number of molecules divided by volume.

rows.label: kinetic-theory assumptions
rows.correct: Ideal-gas molecules are treated as tiny particles in random motion with negligible interactions except brief elastic collisions.
wrong: Ideal-gas molecules continuously exert long-range attractive forces on one another.
rows.explanation: Ideal-gas molecules are treated as tiny particles in random motion with negligible interactions except brief elastic collisions.

rows.label: pressure from molecular motion
rows.correct: Kinetic theory gives P=(1/3)rho vrms squared for an isotropic gas.
wrong: Gas pressure is caused by molecular weight alone and persists without wall collisions.
rows.explanation: Kinetic theory gives P=(1/3)rho vrms squared for an isotropic gas.

rows.label: molecular interpretation of temperature
rows.correct: Average translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)kBT and depends only on absolute temperature.
wrong: At one temperature heavier molecules have greater average translational kinetic energy.
rows.explanation: Average translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)kBT and depends only on absolute temperature.

rows.label: rms molecular speed
rows.correct: Root-mean-square speed is sqrt(3RT/M) for molar mass M in kg per mole.
wrong: RMS speed is proportional to molar mass.
rows.explanation: Root-mean-square speed is sqrt(3RT/M) for molar mass M in kg per mole.

rows.label: pressure from rms speed
rows.correct: Kinetic pressure is one third density times rms speed squared.
wrong: Pressure varies linearly with rms speed.
rows.explanation: Kinetic pressure is one third density times rms speed squared.

rows.label: degrees of freedom
rows.correct: Each independent quadratic translational or rotational degree contributes one half kBT per molecule in classical equilibrium.
wrong: Each degree of freedom contributes kBT per molecule.
rows.explanation: Each independent quadratic translational or rotational degree contributes one half kBT per molecule in classical equilibrium.

rows.label: vibrational modes
rows.correct: Each active vibrational frequency contributes two quadratic modes, kinetic and potential, for total kBT per molecule.
wrong: A vibrational mode contributes only potential energy.
rows.explanation: Each active vibrational frequency contributes two quadratic modes, kinetic and potential, for total kBT per molecule.

rows.label: specific-heat relation
rows.correct: For an ideal gas Cp-Cv=R per mole and gamma=Cp/Cv.
wrong: Cp is smaller than Cv because expansion requires work.
rows.explanation: For an ideal gas Cp-Cv=R per mole and gamma=Cp/Cv.

rows.label: molar internal energy from degrees
rows.correct: For f active quadratic degrees, ideal-gas molar internal energy is (f/2)RT.
wrong: Internal energy is fRT without the one-half factor.
rows.explanation: For f active quadratic degrees, ideal-gas molar internal energy is (f/2)RT.

rows.label: heat-capacity ratio
rows.correct: With f active quadratic degrees, Cv=fR/2 and gamma=(f+2)/f.
wrong: Gamma equals f/2 for every ideal gas.
rows.explanation: With f active quadratic degrees, Cv=fR/2 and gamma=(f+2)/f.

rows.label: mean free path
rows.correct: Mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels between successive collisions.
wrong: Mean free path is the mean distance from a molecule to the container wall only.
rows.explanation: Mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels between successive collisions.

rows.label: collision cross-section
rows.correct: For hard-sphere molecules, larger molecular diameter gives a larger collision cross-section and shorter mean free path.
wrong: Larger molecules at the same number density travel farther between collisions.
rows.explanation: For hard-sphere molecules, larger molecular diameter gives a larger collision cross-section and shorter mean free path.

rows.label: pressure dependence
rows.correct: At fixed temperature, increasing pressure raises number density and reduces mean free path.
wrong: Mean free path increases with pressure at fixed temperature.
rows.explanation: At fixed temperature, increasing pressure raises number density and reduces mean free path.

rows.label: mean free path
rows.correct: For hard spheres, mean free path is 1/(sqrt(2) pi d squared n).
wrong: Mean free path is proportional to molecular diameter squared.
rows.explanation: For hard spheres, mean free path is 1/(sqrt(2) pi d squared n).

rows.label: collision time estimate
rows.correct: Mean collision time is approximately mean free path divided by molecular speed.
wrong: Collision time is mean free path multiplied by speed.
rows.explanation: Mean collision time is approximately mean free path divided by molecular speed.

rows.label: periodic and oscillatory motion
rows.correct: Periodic motion repeats after a fixed interval; oscillatory motion is to-and-fro about an equilibrium position.
wrong: Every periodic motion is necessarily oscillatory along a line.
rows.explanation: Periodic motion repeats after a fixed interval; oscillatory motion is to-and-fro about an equilibrium position.

rows.label: simple harmonic motion
rows.correct: SHM has acceleration proportional to displacement and directed toward equilibrium: a=-omega squared x.
wrong: Any repeating motion is SHM regardless of its force law.
rows.explanation: SHM has acceleration proportional to displacement and directed toward equilibrium: a=-omega squared x.

rows.label: phase and phase constant
rows.correct: The phase omega t plus phi specifies the oscillator state, while phi fixes the initial state for a chosen time origin.
wrong: Two particles with the same amplitude always have the same phase.
rows.explanation: The phase omega t plus phi specifies the oscillator state, while phi fixes the initial state for a chosen time origin.

rows.label: period-frequency relation
rows.correct: Period is the reciprocal of frequency and omega=2 pi f.
wrong: Angular frequency is the same numerical quantity as ordinary frequency.
rows.explanation: Period is the reciprocal of frequency and omega=2 pi f.

rows.label: SHM displacement
rows.correct: For x=A cos(omega t+phi), displacement follows the cosine of phase.
wrong: Amplitude is the instantaneous displacement at every time.
rows.explanation: For x=A cos(omega t+phi), displacement follows the cosine of phase.

rows.label: velocity in SHM
rows.correct: Speed is maximum at equilibrium and zero at the extremes, with v squared=omega squared(A squared-x squared).
wrong: Speed is maximum at maximum displacement.
rows.explanation: Speed is maximum at equilibrium and zero at the extremes, with v squared=omega squared(A squared-x squared).

rows.label: acceleration in SHM
rows.correct: Acceleration is zero at equilibrium and maximum in magnitude at the extremes, always opposing displacement.
wrong: Acceleration and displacement have the same sign in SHM.
rows.explanation: Acceleration is zero at equilibrium and maximum in magnitude at the extremes, always opposing displacement.

rows.label: restoring-force law
rows.correct: A linear restoring force F=-kx produces SHM with angular frequency sqrt(k/m).
wrong: A constant force toward equilibrium produces exact SHM.
rows.explanation: A linear restoring force F=-kx produces SHM with angular frequency sqrt(k/m).

rows.label: SHM speed at displacement
rows.correct: SHM speed magnitude is omega sqrt(A squared-x squared).
wrong: Speed varies linearly as A-x.
rows.explanation: SHM speed magnitude is omega sqrt(A squared-x squared).

rows.label: SHM acceleration
rows.correct: Acceleration is -omega squared x.
wrong: Acceleration is -omega x.
rows.explanation: Acceleration is -omega squared x.

rows.label: energy exchange in SHM
rows.correct: In ideal SHM, kinetic and potential energies exchange while total mechanical energy remains constant.
wrong: Kinetic and potential energies are individually constant in SHM.
rows.explanation: In ideal SHM, kinetic and potential energies exchange while total mechanical energy remains constant.

rows.label: turning points and equilibrium
rows.correct: At a turning point energy is entirely potential, while at equilibrium it is entirely kinetic for a spring oscillator.
wrong: Both kinetic and potential energy vanish at equilibrium.
rows.explanation: At a turning point energy is entirely potential, while at equilibrium it is entirely kinetic for a spring oscillator.

rows.label: energy frequency
rows.correct: Kinetic and potential energies vary with twice the oscillation frequency because they contain squared sine or cosine terms.
wrong: Energy oscillates with half the displacement frequency.
rows.explanation: Kinetic and potential energies vary with twice the oscillation frequency because they contain squared sine or cosine terms.

rows.label: total SHM energy
rows.correct: Total energy of a spring oscillator is one half kA squared.
wrong: Total energy is proportional to amplitude.
rows.explanation: Total energy of a spring oscillator is one half kA squared.

rows.label: spring oscillator period
rows.correct: The period of an ideal mass-spring oscillator is 2 pi sqrt(m/k).
wrong: A heavier mass oscillates faster on the same spring.
rows.explanation: The period of an ideal mass-spring oscillator is 2 pi sqrt(m/k).

rows.label: simple pendulum approximation
rows.correct: For small angular displacement, sin theta is approximately theta and the pendulum executes approximate SHM.
wrong: A simple pendulum is exact SHM at every amplitude.
rows.explanation: For small angular displacement, sin theta is approximately theta and the pendulum executes approximate SHM.

rows.label: pendulum period dependencies
rows.correct: For small oscillations, pendulum period depends on length and local g, not bob mass.
wrong: A heavier pendulum bob has a longer small-angle period.
rows.explanation: For small oscillations, pendulum period depends on length and local g, not bob mass.

rows.label: effective gravity
rows.correct: In an accelerating support, pendulum behaviour is governed by the vector effective gravity.
wrong: Horizontal acceleration changes pendulum mass and therefore its period.
rows.explanation: In an accelerating support, pendulum behaviour is governed by the vector effective gravity.

rows.label: simple pendulum period
rows.correct: Small-angle period is 2 pi sqrt(L/g).
wrong: Pendulum period is proportional to length.
rows.explanation: Small-angle period is 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

rows.label: pendulum length from period
rows.correct: Pendulum length is gT squared divided by 4 pi squared.
wrong: Length is proportional to period rather than period squared.
