rows.explanation: Pendulum length is gT squared divided by 4 pi squared.

rows.label: mechanical wave
rows.correct: A mechanical wave transports energy through a material medium while particles oscillate about equilibrium without net bulk travel with the wave.
wrong: Medium particles move from source to receiver with the wave speed.
rows.explanation: A mechanical wave transports energy through a material medium while particles oscillate about equilibrium without net bulk travel with the wave.

rows.label: transverse and longitudinal waves
rows.correct: Particle displacement is perpendicular to propagation in a transverse wave and parallel in a longitudinal wave.
wrong: Sound in air is transverse because it can be drawn as a sinusoid.
rows.explanation: Particle displacement is perpendicular to propagation in a transverse wave and parallel in a longitudinal wave.

rows.label: travelling-wave phase
rows.correct: For y=A sin(kx-omega t+phi), constant phase moves in the positive x direction.
wrong: The sign between kx and omega t has no relation to propagation direction.
rows.explanation: For y=A sin(kx-omega t+phi), constant phase moves in the positive x direction.

rows.label: wave number and wavelength
rows.correct: Angular wave number is 2 pi divided by wavelength.
wrong: Wave number equals wavelength divided by 2 pi.
rows.explanation: Angular wave number is 2 pi divided by wavelength.

rows.label: phase difference
rows.correct: At one instant, phase difference between points separated by Delta x is 2 pi Delta x/lambda.
wrong: Phase difference depends only on amplitude.
rows.explanation: At one instant, phase difference between points separated by Delta x is 2 pi Delta x/lambda.

rows.label: wave speed relation
rows.correct: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength and is set mainly by medium properties for a mechanical wave.
wrong: Increasing source frequency necessarily increases wave speed in the same nondispersive medium.
rows.explanation: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength and is set mainly by medium properties for a mechanical wave.

rows.label: string-wave speed
rows.correct: Transverse-wave speed on a stretched string is sqrt(T/mu), where mu is linear mass density.
wrong: A heavier string at the same tension carries waves faster.
rows.explanation: Transverse-wave speed on a stretched string is sqrt(T/mu), where mu is linear mass density.

rows.label: speed of sound
rows.correct: Sound speed depends on an elastic modulus divided by density under a square root; in a gas the adiabatic bulk modulus is gamma P.
wrong: Sound speed in a gas is determined by pressure alone and is independent of density.
rows.explanation: Sound speed depends on an elastic modulus divided by density under a square root; in a gas the adiabatic bulk modulus is gamma P.

rows.label: wave speed from frequency
rows.correct: For a periodic wave, v=f lambda.
wrong: Wave speed equals frequency divided by wavelength.
rows.explanation: For a periodic wave, v=f lambda.

rows.label: speed on a stretched string
rows.correct: String-wave speed is sqrt(T/mu).
wrong: String-wave speed is proportional to tension rather than its square root.
rows.explanation: String-wave speed is sqrt(T/mu).

rows.label: superposition and interference
rows.correct: When waves overlap in a linear medium, resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of individual displacements.
wrong: Interfering waves permanently destroy each other after destructive interference.
rows.explanation: When waves overlap in a linear medium, resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of individual displacements.

rows.label: reflection phase change
rows.correct: A transverse wave reflecting from a rigid end undergoes phase reversal, while reflection from a free end does not.
wrong: Reflection from both fixed and free ends always reverses phase.
rows.explanation: A transverse wave reflecting from a rigid end undergoes phase reversal, while reflection from a free end does not.

rows.label: standing-wave nodes and antinodes
rows.correct: Standing waves have fixed nodes of zero amplitude and antinodes of maximum amplitude, with adjacent nodes separated by lambda/2.
wrong: Energy is progressively transported through a perfect standing wave.
rows.explanation: Standing waves have fixed nodes of zero amplitude and antinodes of maximum amplitude, with adjacent nodes separated by lambda/2.

rows.label: resultant interference amplitude
rows.correct: Two equal-amplitude waves of phase difference phi combine with amplitude 2a cos(phi/2) in magnitude.
wrong: Resultant amplitude is always 2a regardless of phase.
rows.explanation: Two equal-amplitude waves of phase difference phi combine with amplitude 2a cos(phi/2) in magnitude.

rows.label: node spacing
rows.correct: Adjacent nodes or adjacent antinodes of a standing wave are separated by lambda/2.
wrong: A node and its nearest antinode are separated by lambda/2.
rows.explanation: Adjacent nodes or adjacent antinodes of a standing wave are separated by lambda/2.

rows.label: harmonics of strings and open pipes
rows.correct: A string fixed at both ends and an open pipe support all integer harmonics with fundamental v/(2L).
wrong: An open pipe supports only odd harmonics.
rows.explanation: A string fixed at both ends and an open pipe support all integer harmonics with fundamental v/(2L).

rows.label: closed-pipe harmonics
rows.correct: A pipe closed at one end supports odd harmonics with fundamental v/(4L) in the ideal end-correction-free model.
wrong: The second harmonic is an allowed mode of an ideal one-end-closed pipe.
rows.explanation: A pipe closed at one end supports odd harmonics with fundamental v/(4L) in the ideal end-correction-free model.

rows.label: beats and resonance
rows.correct: Beats have frequency equal to the absolute difference of two nearby frequencies; resonance gives large response near a natural frequency.
wrong: Beat frequency is the sum of the two source frequencies.
rows.explanation: Beats have frequency equal to the absolute difference of two nearby frequencies; resonance gives large response near a natural frequency.

rows.label: fixed-string frequency
rows.correct: Allowed string frequencies are nv/(2L).
wrong: The fundamental of a fixed string is v/(4L).
rows.explanation: Allowed string frequencies are nv/(2L).

rows.label: beat frequency
rows.correct: Beat frequency is the absolute difference between nearby component frequencies.
wrong: Beat frequency is their arithmetic mean.
rows.explanation: Beat frequency is the absolute difference between nearby component frequencies.

rows.label: quantisation of charge
rows.correct: The charge on any observable body occurs in integral multiples of the elementary charge e.
wrong: The integer n may take any fractional value.
Quantisation means charge can be created from nothing.
The elementary charge varies with the size of a body.
rows.explanation: The charge on any observable body occurs in integral multiples of the elementary charge e.

rows.label: conservation of charge
rows.correct: The total charge of an isolated system remains constant.
wrong: Charge disappears whenever bodies are earthed.
Each object must retain its original charge.
Conservation requires the number of particles to remain fixed.
rows.explanation: The total charge of an isolated system remains constant.

rows.label: additivity of charge
rows.correct: The total charge is the algebraic sum of individual charges.
wrong: Charges add according to the parallelogram law.
Only magnitudes of charges are added.
Charge addition depends on their separation.
rows.explanation: The total charge is the algebraic sum of individual charges.

rows.label: Coulomb force direction
rows.correct: The electrostatic force between two point charges acts along their joining line.
wrong: The force is always perpendicular to the joining line.
Both interaction forces point in the same direction.
Unlike charges repel in vacuum.
rows.explanation: The electrostatic force between two point charges acts along their joining line.

rows.label: permittivity effect
rows.correct: A dielectric medium changes electrostatic force through its permittivity.
wrong: A dielectric always increases Coulomb force by K.
Permittivity has no role in electrostatic interaction.
Relative permittivity of vacuum is zero.
rows.explanation: A dielectric medium changes electrostatic force through its permittivity.

rows.label: superposition principle
rows.correct: The net force or field is the vector sum of contributions from individual sources.
wrong: Only the nearest charge contributes.
Field magnitudes are always added arithmetically.
Superposition changes the charge of each source.
rows.explanation: The net force or field is the vector sum of contributions from individual sources.

rows.label: electric field
rows.correct: Electric field at a point is force per unit positive test charge in the limit of a vanishingly small test charge.
wrong: It depends on the magnitude of the chosen test charge.
Its SI unit is coulomb per newton.
It is a scalar potential.
rows.explanation: Electric field at a point is force per unit positive test charge in the limit of a vanishingly small test charge.

rows.label: field of a positive point charge
rows.correct: The electric field of a positive point charge is radially outward.
wrong: It is radially inward.
Its magnitude varies as r².
It is uniform throughout space.
rows.explanation: The electric field of a positive point charge is radially outward.

rows.label: electric field lines
rows.correct: Electric field lines are curves whose tangent gives the field direction.
wrong: They can cross at points where the field is strong.
They form closed loops in electrostatics.
They begin on negative charge and end on positive charge.
rows.explanation: Electric field lines are curves whose tangent gives the field direction.

rows.label: electric flux
rows.correct: Electric flux through a surface measures the surface integral of E·dA.
wrong: It is always equal to EA regardless of orientation.
It is a vector parallel to the area vector.
It depends only on the perimeter of the surface.
rows.explanation: Electric flux through a surface measures the surface integral of E·dA.

rows.label: electric dipole moment
rows.correct: Dipole moment equals charge magnitude times the displacement vector from negative to positive charge.
wrong: Its direction is from +q to −q.
Its SI unit is C/m.
It is independent of charge separation.
rows.explanation: Dipole moment equals charge magnitude times the displacement vector from negative to positive charge.

rows.label: axial dipole field
rows.correct: Far from a dipole, the axial electric field points along the dipole moment and varies as 1/r³.
wrong: It varies as 1/r².
It always points opposite to the dipole moment.
It equals the field of a point charge with charge p.
rows.explanation: Far from a dipole, the axial electric field points along the dipole moment and varies as 1/r³.

rows.label: equatorial dipole field
rows.correct: Far from a dipole, the equatorial electric field points opposite to the dipole moment.
wrong: It points along the dipole moment.
It varies as 1/r.
It is zero everywhere on the equatorial line.
rows.explanation: Far from a dipole, the equatorial electric field points opposite to the dipole moment.

rows.label: dipole torque
rows.correct: A dipole in a uniform electric field experiences torque p × E.
wrong: Torque is maximum when p is parallel to E.
A uniform field always exerts a nonzero net force on a dipole.
Stable equilibrium occurs when p is antiparallel to E.
rows.explanation: A dipole in a uniform electric field experiences torque p × E.
rows.section: 1.11 Dipole in a Uniform External Field

rows.label: linear charge density
rows.correct: Linear charge density is charge per unit length.
wrong: It is charge per unit area.
Its SI unit is C m⁻².
It can describe only point charges.
rows.explanation: Linear charge density is charge per unit length.

rows.label: surface charge density
rows.correct: Surface charge density is charge per unit area.
wrong: It is charge per unit volume.
Its SI unit is C m⁻³.
It must be uniform on every surface.
rows.explanation: Surface charge density is charge per unit area.

rows.label: Gauss’s law
rows.correct: The net electric flux through any closed surface equals enclosed charge divided by ε₀.
wrong: External charges contribute to the net enclosed charge.
It applies only to spherical surfaces.
Zero enclosed charge requires zero field everywhere on the surface.
rows.explanation: The net electric flux through any closed surface equals enclosed charge divided by ε₀.

rows.label: Gaussian surface
rows.correct: A Gaussian surface is an imaginary closed surface chosen to exploit field symmetry.
wrong: It must coincide with a charged body.
It may be an open surface.
Its shape changes the enclosed physical charge.
rows.explanation: A Gaussian surface is an imaginary closed surface chosen to exploit field symmetry.

rows.label: field of an infinite line charge
rows.correct: The electric field of a uniform infinite line charge is radial and proportional to 1/r.
wrong: The field is proportional to 1/r².
The field is parallel to the line.
A spherical Gaussian surface is required by law.
rows.explanation: The electric field of a uniform infinite line charge is radial and proportional to 1/r.

rows.label: field inside a charged spherical shell
rows.correct: The electrostatic field everywhere inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell is zero.
wrong: The inside field grows linearly with radius.
The inside field equals kQ/R² everywhere.
The outside field is uniform.
rows.explanation: The electrostatic field everywhere inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell is zero.

rows.label: electrostatic potential
rows.correct: Potential at a point is the work done per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity without acceleration.
wrong: Potential is force per unit charge.
Potential is a vector directed along the field.
Potential at every point must be positive.
rows.explanation: Potential at a point is the work done per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity without acceleration.

rows.label: potential difference
rows.correct: Potential difference equals the negative line integral of electric field between two points.
wrong: It depends on the chosen path in electrostatics.
Potential necessarily increases along an electric field line.
Its unit is newton per coulomb.
rows.explanation: Potential difference equals the negative line integral of electric field between two points.

rows.label: potential of a point charge
rows.correct: The potential of a point charge Q at distance r is kQ/r with zero at infinity.
wrong: It varies as 1/r².
It is always positive because distance is positive.
It has a direction radial to the charge.
rows.explanation: The potential of a point charge Q at distance r is kQ/r with zero at infinity.
rows.section: 2.3 Potential Due to a Point Charge

rows.label: dipole potential
rows.correct: At a far point, dipole potential is proportional to p cosθ/r².
wrong: It varies as 1/r³ at every far point.
It is maximum on the equatorial plane.
It is independent of orientation.
rows.explanation: At a far point, dipole potential is proportional to p cosθ/r².
rows.section: 2.4 Potential Due to an Electric Dipole

rows.label: potential superposition
rows.correct: Potential due to many point charges is the algebraic sum of their individual potentials.
wrong: Only the nearest charge contributes to potential.
Potential magnitudes are added after discarding signs.
Potential superposition is a vector law.
rows.explanation: Potential due to many point charges is the algebraic sum of their individual potentials.
rows.section: 2.5 Potential Due to a System of Charges

rows.label: equipotential surface
rows.correct: Every point on an equipotential surface has the same potential.
wrong: Electric field is tangent to it.
Equipotential surfaces can intersect.
Charge must move faster along it.
rows.explanation: Every point on an equipotential surface has the same potential.

rows.label: potential energy of two charges
rows.correct: The electrostatic potential energy of two point charges is kq₁q₂/r.
wrong: It is always positive.
It varies as 1/r².
It is a vector along the joining line.
rows.explanation: The electrostatic potential energy of two point charges is kq₁q₂/r.
rows.section: 2.7 Potential Energy of a System of Charges

rows.label: energy of a charge system
rows.correct: The potential energy of a system is obtained by summing each distinct charge pair once.
wrong: Every pair must be counted twice.
Only adjacent charge pairs are included.
The result cannot be negative.
rows.explanation: The potential energy of a system is obtained by summing each distinct charge pair once.
rows.section: 2.7 Potential Energy of a System of Charges

rows.label: dipole energy in an external field
rows.correct: The potential energy of a dipole in a uniform external field is −p·E.
wrong: It is minimum when p is perpendicular to E.
It is pE sinθ.
It is independent of dipole orientation.
rows.explanation: The potential energy of a dipole in a uniform external field is −p·E.
rows.section: 2.8 Potential Energy in an External Field

rows.label: electrostatic equilibrium in a conductor
rows.correct: The electric field inside a conductor is zero in electrostatic equilibrium.
wrong: A steady nonzero field persists inside the conductor.
Excess static charge is uniformly distributed through its volume.
Potential must be zero inside every conductor.
rows.explanation: The electric field inside a conductor is zero in electrostatic equilibrium.

rows.label: field at a conductor surface
rows.correct: Just outside a conductor, the electrostatic field is normal to the surface.
wrong: The field must be tangent to the surface.
Its normal component is always zero.
It is unrelated to surface charge density.
rows.explanation: Just outside a conductor, the electrostatic field is normal to the surface.

rows.label: electrostatic shielding
rows.correct: A closed conducting enclosure shields its cavity from external electrostatic fields.
wrong: A plastic shell provides perfect electrostatic shielding by the same mechanism.
The cavity field must equal the external field.
Shielding requires the conductor to carry net charge.
rows.explanation: A closed conducting enclosure shields its cavity from external electrostatic fields.

rows.label: polarisation of a dielectric
rows.correct: An external electric field produces or aligns electric dipoles in a dielectric.
wrong: Free conduction charges flow indefinitely through an ideal dielectric.
Polarisation always makes the internal field larger.
Molecules lose all electric charge.
rows.explanation: An external electric field produces or aligns electric dipoles in a dielectric.

rows.label: capacitance
rows.correct: Capacitance is the ratio Q/V for a conductor or capacitor geometry.
wrong: It necessarily increases with stored charge at fixed geometry.
Its SI unit is coulomb.
It is defined as V/Q.
rows.explanation: Capacitance is the ratio Q/V for a conductor or capacitor geometry.

rows.label: parallel-plate capacitance
rows.correct: For large closely spaced plates in vacuum, C = ε₀A/d.
wrong: Capacitance is proportional to separation.
Capacitance is independent of plate area.
Fringing is essential to the ideal formula.
rows.explanation: For large closely spaced plates in vacuum, C = ε₀A/d.

rows.label: dielectric in a capacitor
rows.correct: A dielectric filling the gap increases capacitance by its relative permittivity K.
wrong: It decreases capacitance to C/K.
Both charge and voltage must remain fixed in every setup.
The dielectric has no effect on electric field.
rows.explanation: A dielectric filling the gap increases capacitance by its relative permittivity K.

rows.label: capacitors in series
rows.correct: Series capacitors carry equal charge magnitude in electrostatic steady state.
wrong: They all have equal potential difference regardless of capacitance.
Equivalent capacitance is the arithmetic sum.
Each capacitor stores a different series charge supplied through it.
rows.explanation: Series capacitors carry equal charge magnitude in electrostatic steady state.

rows.label: capacitors in parallel
rows.correct: Parallel capacitors have the same potential difference.
wrong: They necessarily carry equal charges.
Equivalent capacitance is less than every branch capacitance.
Their potential differences add in series fashion.
rows.explanation: Parallel capacitors have the same potential difference.

rows.label: energy stored in a capacitor
rows.correct: The energy stored is ½CV² = Q²/(2C) = ½QV.
wrong: Stored energy is CV².
Energy is proportional to V at fixed C.
Energy density is ε₀E.
rows.explanation: The energy stored is ½CV² = Q²/(2C) = ½QV.

rows.label: effect of disconnecting a battery
rows.correct: After a charged capacitor is disconnected from its battery, its charge remains fixed ideally.
wrong: Its voltage must remain fixed by the absent battery.
Its charge immediately becomes zero.
Energy is always proportional to C after disconnection.
rows.explanation: After a charged capacitor is disconnected from its battery, its charge remains fixed ideally.

rows.label: electric current
rows.correct: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge through a cross-section.
wrong: It is total charge multiplied by time.
It is a vector because it has a direction.
Electrons drift in the conventional-current direction.
rows.explanation: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge through a cross-section.

rows.label: steady current
rows.correct: A steady current has the same value through every cross-section of a series path.
wrong: It requires carriers to move at the speed of light.
It means individual electrons have identical velocities.
It can exist only in a perfect conductor.
